sections.p12.s0: The container and CI basics you need before shipping the stack. Work through items 0 to 8 with one small FastAPI app, rebuilding and running it after each change, then set up CI and releases on the same repository. Most items take an evening; Compose and CI take longer.
sections.p12.s1: Your API, database, cache and worker running from one command, tested in CI, and reachable online. Build in order: Compose file, slim Dockerfile, health checks, migrations, CI, the one command, then the deploy. Check each step from a clean state with docker compose down -v before moving on.

p12.s0.0.how: Pull python:3.12-slim, start two containers from it, write a file in one, and confirm the other cannot see it. Then create a named volume, mount it in both, and repeat. Use docker ps -a, docker images and docker volume ls as you go.
p12.s0.0.done: You can explain in one sentence each what an image, a container and a volume are, and which one survives docker rm.

p12.s0.1.how: Write a Dockerfile for a small FastAPI app that copies the whole project, then build it twice after editing one source file. Reorder it to copy and install requirements.txt before the source, add a .dockerignore, and rebuild after the same edit.
p12.s0.1.done: After a source-only edit the rebuild shows the dependency layer as CACHED and finishes in seconds.

p12.s0.2.how: Split the Dockerfile into a builder stage that installs dependencies into a virtual environment and a final python:3.12-slim stage that copies only that environment and your code. Compare sizes with docker images.
p12.s0.2.done: The final image is noticeably smaller than the single-stage one and contains no compilers or build tools.

p12.s0.3.how: Add a user with useradd in the Dockerfile, chown the app directory, and switch with USER. Run whoami through docker exec and try to write to a root-owned path to see it refused.
p12.s0.3.done: whoami inside the container prints your app user, not root, and the app still starts.

p12.s0.4.how: Run PostgreSQL with a named volume for its data directory, remove and recreate the container, and confirm the data is still there. Then run your app with a bind mount of the source folder and uvicorn --reload, and edit a file on the host.
p12.s0.4.done: Database data survives container removal, and host edits reload the app without a rebuild.

p12.s0.5.how: Create a user-defined network with docker network create, start PostgreSQL and your app on it, and connect from the app using the container name as host. Then try the same on the default bridge network and note the difference.
p12.s0.5.done: Your app reaches the database by name, and you can explain why localhost inside a container does not mean the host.

p12.s0.6.how: Write a compose.yaml for your app and PostgreSQL with a named volume, then run docker compose up, logs, ps and down. Add depends_on with condition: service_healthy.
p12.s0.6.done: docker compose up starts both services with the app waiting for a healthy database, and down removes them cleanly.

p12.s0.7.how: Move all settings to environment variables read by your app, and supply them from a .env file listed in .gitignore and .dockerignore. Run docker history on your image to confirm no secret appears in any layer.
p12.s0.7.done: The image contains no keys or passwords, and you can say why ENV or ARG with a secret leaks it.

p12.s0.8.how: Add a /health endpoint and a healthcheck in Compose that calls it, plus restart: unless-stopped. Make the endpoint fail on purpose and watch docker compose ps report the service as unhealthy.
p12.s0.8.done: You can make the service show healthy and unhealthy on demand, and it restarts after you kill its process.

p12.s0.9.how: Add .github/workflows/ci.yml that runs on push and pull request: set up Python, install dependencies, then run pytest, ruff check and mypy. Push a commit that breaks a test to see the run fail.
p12.s0.9.done: Every push shows a green or red check on GitHub, and the broken commit turns it red.

p12.s0.10.how: Add a workflow triggered by pushing a tag such as v0.1.0 that builds the image, tags it with the version, and pushes it to GitHub Container Registry. Write down the deploy step as a single command that pulls a given tag.
p12.s0.10.done: Pushing a new tag produces an image with that tag in the registry, and deploying an older tag rolls back.

p12.s1.0.how: Write compose.yaml with four services: api (FastAPI), db (postgres with a named volume), redis, and worker built from the same image with a different command. Wire them with environment variables and bring it up.
p12.s1.0.done: docker compose ps shows all four running, and a request to the API that queues a job gets processed by the worker.

p12.s1.1.how: Use a multi-stage build on python:3.12-slim, install only runtime dependencies in the final stage, add a .dockerignore, and set a non-root USER. Check size with docker images and remove what you do not need until it fits.
p12.s1.1.done: docker images reports under 200MB and docker compose exec api whoami prints a non-root user.

p12.s1.2.how: Add a healthcheck to each service: pg_isready for PostgreSQL, redis-cli ping for Redis, an HTTP call to /health for the API, and a heartbeat check for the worker. Use condition: service_healthy in depends_on.
p12.s1.2.done: docker compose ps shows every service as healthy, and stopping the database turns the API unhealthy.

p12.s1.3.how: Manage schema with Alembic and run alembic upgrade head in a one-off migrate service that the API waits for with service_completed_successfully. Keep migrations backward-compatible so an old API still works against the new schema.
p12.s1.3.done: Starting the stack twice in a row runs migrations once and succeeds both times, and scaling the API to two replicas does not run them twice.

p12.s1.4.how: Extend the CI workflow: run ruff, mypy and pytest with a PostgreSQL service container, then build the image with docker/build-push-action. Make the build job depend on the test job with needs.
p12.s1.4.done: A push runs lint, types, tests and the image build, and a failing test stops the build job.

p12.s1.5.how: Write a README section and a script or Makefile target that copies .env.example if needed and runs docker compose up --build -d. Test it from a fresh clone after docker compose down -v and docker system prune.
p12.s1.5.done: On a fresh clone the one command brings the stack to all-healthy with no manual steps.

p12.s1.6.how: Rent a small VPS or use a container host such as Fly.io or Render. Pull your tagged image, set secrets through the host's secret store, put HTTPS in front, and expose only the API port. Keep the database off the public internet.
p12.s1.6.done: curl https://your-domain/health from another network returns 200, and the database port is not reachable from outside.
